about: 1P2 Materials is the Part IA Engineering Tripos course on engineering materials. According to the 2025–26 syllabus page (the 2026–27 page could not be checked), it is taught as one Michaelmas lecture, a Christmas-vacation 'Teach Yourself' examples paper, 12 Lent lectures and 4 Easter lectures, with some material delivered online. It covers mechanical properties and stress analysis, the microstructural origins of stiffness and strength, fracture, fatigue, friction and wear, and material and process selection with environmental impact; the recommended texts are by Ashby, Shercliff and Cebon, Ashby and Jones, and Callister. It is examined with Structural Mechanics in Paper 2 (Structures and Materials), one of four 3-hour Part IA papers.
topics: Material classes, mechanical properties and their measurement
Stress and strain analysis: 3D Hooke's law, constrained deformation and thermal stress
Physical basis of elastic modulus; foams and composites
Plasticity: dislocations, strengthening of metals, and yielding and failure of polymers
Toughness, fracture toughness and fracture mechanisms
Fatigue and Weibull statistics for ceramics
Material and process selection in design

notes.h: Material classes, mechanical properties and their measurement
notes.body:
1P2 Materials links what materials are made of to how they behave, and then uses that to choose materials for designs. It starts by defining the properties that matter.

Classes of engineering materials
- Metals: stiff, strong, ductile and tough, but dense and often prone to corrosion.
- Ceramics and glasses: stiff, hard and heat-resistant but brittle, with low toughness.
- Polymers: light and easy to shape, but much less stiff than metals and ceramics, and their properties depend strongly on temperature.
- Elastomers: very low stiffness and very large recoverable strains.
- Hybrids: composites, foams and natural materials such as wood, combining two or more of the above.

The tensile test
A specimen of original length L₀ and area A₀ is pulled while load F and extension ΔL are recorded.
- Nominal (engineering) stress σn = F/A₀; nominal strain εn = ΔL/L₀.
- Young's modulus E is the slope of the initial linear (elastic) part.
- Yield strength σy marks the start of permanent (plastic) deformation. Where there is no sharp yield point, a 0.1% or 0.2% proof stress is used.
- Tensile strength σts is the maximum nominal stress (maximum load/A₀). Beyond it the specimen necks and the load falls.
- Ductility is the plastic strain at fracture, εf.
- Unloading from the plastic region follows a line of slope E, so only the elastic strain is recovered.

True stress and strain
- Once strains are large, A changes noticeably. True stress σt = F/A; true strain εt = ln(L/L₀).
- Plastic flow conserves volume (AL = A₀L₀), so σt = σn(1 + εn) and εt = ln(1 + εn).
- Example: σn = 400 MPa at εn = 0.2 gives σt = 480 MPa and εt = ln 1.2 ≈ 0.18.

Hardness
- A hardness test presses a hard indenter into the surface: H = load/projected contact area. It is quick and almost non-destructive.
- For metals H ≈ 3σy, because the constrained material under the indenter must flow plastically.

Property charts
- Ashby charts plot one property against another on logarithmic axes, e.g. Young's modulus against density. Each class forms a "bubble".
- Typical values: steels E ≈ 200–210 GPa and ρ ≈ 7.8 Mg/m³; aluminium alloys about 70 GPa and 2.7 Mg/m³; polymers roughly 0.2–4 GPa and 0.9–1.5 Mg/m³; elastomers below about 0.01 GPa.
- The charts make it easy to see trade-offs and are used later for material selection.

Exam tips: always state whether you are using nominal or true quantities; the most common slip is using A₀ when the question needs the current area.

notes.h: Stress and strain analysis: 3D Hooke's law, constrained deformation and thermal stress
notes.body:
Hooke's law in three dimensions
For an isotropic linear-elastic material with principal stresses σ₁, σ₂, σ₃ and a temperature change ΔT:
- ε₁ = [σ₁ − ν(σ₂ + σ₃)]/E + αΔT, and similarly for ε₂ and ε₃.
- ν is Poisson's ratio (about 0.3 for most metals, close to 0.5 for rubbers, which are nearly incompressible); α is the linear thermal expansion coefficient.
- The shear modulus is G = E/[2(1 + ν)] and the bulk modulus K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)]. For ν = 0.3, G ≈ 0.38E and K ≈ 0.83E.

The method for constrained problems
1. Write the 3D Hooke's law equations.
2. Insert what you know: zero stress on free surfaces; zero strain (or a known strain) where something is constrained.
3. Solve for the unknown stresses and strains.

Example: lateral constraint
A block is loaded by σ₁ while sitting in a rigid channel that prevents expansion in direction 2 (direction 3 is free, so σ₃ = 0).
- ε₂ = 0 gives σ₂ = νσ₁: the channel pushes back.
- Then ε₁ = (σ₁ − ν²σ₁)/E = σ₁(1 − ν²)/E, so the block appears stiffer, with effective modulus E/(1 − ν²). For steel (E = 210 GPa, ν = 0.3) that is about 231 GPa.

Thermal stress
- A free body heated by ΔT simply expands with strain αΔT and has no stress.
- A bar held between rigid walls cannot expand: 0 = σ/E + αΔT, so σ = −EαΔT (compressive on heating).
- Example: steel, E = 210 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, ΔT = 50 K: σ = −210 × 10⁹ × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = −126 MPa.
- A thin coating bonded to a much thicker substrate is constrained equally in both in-plane directions. Setting ε₁ = ε₂ = (difference in thermal strain) and σ₃ = 0 gives σ = −EΔαΔT/(1 − ν), where Δα is the mismatch in expansion coefficients.

Compound bars
When two materials are joined and must deform together:
- Compatibility: both have the same total strain.
- Equilibrium: the internal forces sum to zero (with no external load).
- Example: equal-area steel (E = 210 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and aluminium (E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) bars joined at their ends and heated by 100 K. Equal and opposite stresses σ satisfy σ/Es + αsΔT = −σ/Ea + αaΔT, so σ = (αa − αs)ΔT/(1/Es + 1/Ea) ≈ 58 MPa: tension in the steel and compression in the aluminium.

Why it matters
Thermal stresses cause cracking in ceramics on rapid cooling (thermal shock), distort welded structures, and set the limits for joining dissimilar materials, as in electronic packaging and coated turbine blades.

Exam tips: write all three Hooke's law equations even if one direction looks trivial, and state clearly which stresses are zero and which strains are constrained before solving.

This part of the course is partly taught through an online "Teach Yourself" Guided Learning Unit, so make sure you work through it.

Atomic bonding
- Primary (strong) bonds: ionic (electrostatic attraction between ions, e.g. in many ceramics), covalent (shared electron pairs, e.g. diamond, silicon carbide, and along polymer chains), and metallic (ions in a "sea" of free electrons, giving ductility and conductivity).
- Secondary (weak) bonds: van der Waals and hydrogen bonds. They hold polymer chains to each other, so they control the stiffness of polymers.

Crystal structures of metals
Many metals pack their atoms in one of three structures:
- Face-centred cubic (FCC): atoms at the cube corners and face centres; 4 atoms per unit cell; each atom has 12 nearest neighbours; packing fraction 0.74. Examples: aluminium, copper, nickel, austenitic stainless steel.
- Body-centred cubic (BCC): atoms at the corners and the cube centre; 2 atoms per cell; 8 nearest neighbours; packing fraction 0.68. Examples: iron at room temperature (ferrite), chromium, tungsten.
- Close-packed hexagonal (CPH, also called HCP): packing fraction 0.74. Examples: magnesium, titanium at room temperature, zinc.
- FCC and CPH are both stackings of close-packed planes; they differ only in the stacking sequence (ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for CPH). In FCC the close-packed planes are the {111} family.

Geometry of the unit cell
- In FCC, atoms touch along a face diagonal: 4r = √2 a.
- In BCC, atoms touch along a body diagonal: 4r = √3 a.

Density from first principles
- ρ = (atoms per cell × atomic mass)/(N_A × cell volume) = nA_r/(N_A a³), with atomic mass in kg/mol.
- Copper (FCC, a = 0.3615 nm, 63.55 g/mol): ρ = 4 × 0.06355/(6.022 × 10²³ × (0.3615 × 10⁻⁹)³) ≈ 8.94 × 10³ kg/m³, close to the measured 8.96 Mg/m³.
- Aluminium (FCC, a = 0.405 nm, 26.98 g/mol) gives about 2.70 Mg/m³.
- Density is controlled mainly by atomic mass, with packing a secondary effect. That is why light alloys are based on light elements (Mg, Al, Ti).

Polymers
- Long chain molecules with a covalently bonded carbon backbone.
- Thermoplastics: chains held together by secondary bonds; they soften on heating and can be remoulded. They may be amorphous or partly crystalline.
- Thermosets: chains densely cross-linked by covalent bonds (e.g. epoxy).
- Elastomers: lightly cross-linked polymers used above their glass transition temperature Tg.
- Polymers are light (about 0.9–1.5 Mg/m³) because they are made of light atoms (C, H, O) and pack loosely.

Microstructural length scales
Properties are controlled on many scales: atomic bonding and crystal structure (sub-nanometre), dislocations and precipitates (nanometres), grains (micrometres) and component geometry and defects (millimetres and up).

Exam tips: for density questions, write the formula in words first, then substitute in SI units; converting a from nm to m and the atomic mass from g to kg are the usual pitfalls.

notes.h: Physical basis of elastic modulus; foams and composites
notes.body:
Bonds as springs
- The energy of two atoms varies with separation r, with a minimum at the equilibrium spacing r₀. The force is F = dU/dr.
- For small displacements each bond behaves like a spring of stiffness S = d²U/dr² at r₀.
- A simple model of atoms on a cubic grid gives E ≈ S/r₀. With S ≈ 50 N/m and r₀ ≈ 0.25 nm, E ≈ 200 GPa, the right order for steel.
- Strong primary bonds (covalent, ionic, metallic) give E in the tens to hundreds of GPa (diamond about 1000 GPa).

Polymers and elastomers
- Below Tg, a polymer's stiffness is set mainly by the weak secondary bonds between chains: E of order a few GPa.
- Above Tg, the secondary bonds have "melted": the stiffness collapses by orders of magnitude. If the chains are cross-linked, the material becomes an elastomer, whose stiffness comes from the entropy of the coiled chains and rises with cross-link density (rubbers have E of order 1–10 MPa).
- So polymer stiffness is very temperature-sensitive near Tg, which is a key design limitation.

Modulus is hard to change by alloying
Because E depends on bonding, small additions of alloying elements or heat treatment barely change it: all steels have E ≈ 200–210 GPa. To get a different modulus you need a different material, or a hybrid.

Composites
A composite combines reinforcement (fibres or particles) of modulus E_f in a matrix E_m, with volume fraction f of reinforcement.
- Density follows the rule of mixtures exactly: ρ = fρ_f + (1 − f)ρ_m.
- Loaded along continuous aligned fibres, both phases have the same strain (Voigt, upper bound): E = fE_f + (1 − f)E_m.
- Loaded across the fibres, both carry the same stress (Reuss, lower bound): 1/E = f/E_f + (1 − f)/E_m.
- Example: glass fibre (72 GPa) in epoxy (3 GPa) at f = 0.5 gives about 37.5 GPa along the fibres but only about 5.8 GPa across them: composites are strongly anisotropic. Real particulate composites fall between the bounds.

Foams
- A foam is a network of cell walls or struts with relative density ρ̃ = ρ/ρ_s (foam density over solid density).
- When loaded, the struts bend, which is much more compliant than stretching. Analysis of strut bending gives E ≈ E_s(ρ/ρ_s)² for open-cell foams.
- So a foam at 10% relative density has about 1% of the solid's modulus.
- Foams fill large regions of property charts that solids cannot reach and are used for cushioning, insulation and sandwich-panel cores.

Exam tips: for composites, sketch the two loading geometries and state "equal strain" or "equal stress" before writing the bound; examiners look for the physical argument.

notes.h: Plasticity: dislocations, strengthening of metals, and yielding and failure of polymers
notes.body:
Ideal strength
- If a perfect crystal yielded by sliding whole planes of atoms over one another, the shear stress needed would be of order G/10 (simple estimates range from about G/30 to G/6).
- Measured yield strengths of pure metals are hundreds or thousands of times lower. The explanation is dislocations.

Dislocations
- A dislocation is a line defect: an extra half-plane of atoms (edge dislocation) or a spiral shift of planes (screw dislocation). The Burgers vector b is the slip it produces.
- Plastic flow happens when dislocations glide on slip planes, breaking and remaking only a row of bonds at a time. This is why yield is so much easier than the ideal estimate.
- A shear stress τ exerts a force τb per unit length on a dislocation.
- Dislocations have a line tension T ≈ ½Gb².
- Metals with FCC structure (many slip systems on close-packed planes) are typically ductile.

Strength of a polycrystal
- The shear stress needed to move dislocations on a slip system is the dislocation yield strength τy (the critical resolved shear stress).
- In a polycrystal the grains are randomly oriented, so the applied tensile stress is resolved onto most slip systems less favourably than in a well-oriented single crystal, and each grain must deform compatibly with its neighbours. The result is σy ≈ 3τy.
- The factor relating the polycrystal's tensile yield strength to the critical resolved shear stress is the Taylor factor. For randomly oriented FCC polycrystals it is about 3.06, rounded to 3 in simple estimates.

Strengthening mechanisms
To make a metal stronger, put obstacles in the way of dislocations.
- Obstacles with spacing L: a dislocation bows between them, and breaks through when τbL = 2T, giving τ ≈ Gb/L. Closer obstacles mean higher strength. Example: G = 80 GPa, b = 0.25 nm, L = 100 nm gives τ ≈ 200 MPa and σy ≈ 600 MPa.
- Solid solution strengthening: dissolved atoms of a different size distort the lattice (e.g. zinc in copper to make brass).
- Precipitation and dispersion strengthening: fine particles of a second phase, produced by heat treatment (e.g. age-hardened aluminium alloys) or added as dispersions.
- Work hardening: plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which tangle and obstruct each other. Cold-worked metal is stronger but less ductile; annealing reverses it.
- Grain boundary strengthening: boundaries block slip. Hall–Petch: σy = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2), so finer grains give higher strength.
- Mechanisms add, so commercial alloys combine several.
- Processing sets the microstructure: alloy composition, heat treatment and deformation work together.

Yielding of polymers
- Polymers have no crystal dislocations. Glassy polymers yield by shear yielding (chains sliding past one another, often in localised shear bands) or, in tension, by crazing: microscopic cracks bridged by stretched fibrils, which can lead to brittle fracture.
- Yield strength depends strongly on temperature and strain rate: polymers are stronger when cold or loaded quickly.
- Above Tg, thermoplastics flow viscously; below it they may be brittle.

Exam tips: be ready to explain, with a sketch, why real yield strengths are far below the ideal strength, and to name an example alloy for each strengthening mechanism.

notes.h: Toughness, fracture toughness and fracture mechanisms
notes.body:
Strength is not enough: a component can fail at a stress well below its yield strength if it contains a crack. Fracture mechanics tells us when a crack will run.

Definitions
- Toughness G_c (J/m²) is the energy absorbed per unit area of crack advance.
- The stress intensity factor K = Yσ√(πa) characterises the stress field at a crack tip, where σ is the remote stress, a is the crack length (half-length for an internal crack) and Y is a geometry factor (about 1 for a centre crack in a wide plate, about 1.1 for an edge crack).
- Fast fracture occurs when K reaches the fracture toughness K_c (MPa√m), a material property.
- The two are linked: K_c ≈ √(EG_c).

Typical values (orders of magnitude)
- Tough metals such as many steels: K_c of tens to over 100 MPa√m.
- Ceramics and glass: about 1–5 MPa√m (glass under 1).
- Unreinforced polymers: about 1–5 MPa√m, but polymers have low E, so their G_c can be comparable to that of ceramics or higher.
- Using K_c ≈ √(EG_c): steel with E = 200 GPa and G_c = 10 kJ/m² gives about 45 MPa√m; glass with E = 70 GPa and G_c = 10 J/m² gives about 0.84 MPa√m.

Design against fast fracture
- Three quantities interact: stress, crack size and K_c. Fix any two and the third follows.
- Critical crack size: a_c = (1/π)(K_c/Yσ)².
- Example: K_c = 50 MPa√m, σ = 300 MPa, Y = 1: a_c = (1/π)(50/300)² ≈ 8.8 mm.
- Non-destructive testing finds cracks; design must ensure the largest crack that could be missed is below a_c.
- For pressure vessels, "leak before break" design ensures a through-thickness crack leaks (and is detected) before it reaches the critical length.

Micromechanisms
- Ductile fracture in metals: a plastic zone forms at the crack tip; voids nucleate at inclusions, grow and link up. Lots of plastic work, so G_c is high. Fracture surfaces look dimpled.
- The plastic zone size scales as (K/σy)². The simplest estimate is r_p ≈ K²/(2πσy²) (some texts use a factor of 1/π). High-strength alloys with low toughness have small plastic zones.
- Brittle fracture (cleavage) in ceramics and in some metals at low temperature: the crack splits atomic planes with little plasticity, giving flat, faceted surfaces.
- BCC metals, including ordinary ferritic steels, show a ductile-to-brittle transition as temperature falls; FCC metals such as aluminium and copper do not.
- Toughness can fall with increasing yield strength, so the strongest alloy is not always the safest choice.

Exam tips: check units carefully in K = Yσ√(πa): with σ in MPa and a in metres, K comes out in MPa√m; a crack length in millimetres must be converted first.

notes.h: Fatigue and Weibull statistics for ceramics
notes.body:
Fatigue
Fatigue is failure under cyclic loading at stresses below the static strength. It causes a large share of mechanical failures in service.

Describing the loading
- Stress range Δσ = σmax − σmin; amplitude σa = Δσ/2; mean stress σm = (σmax + σmin)/2; load ratio R = σmin/σmax.

Uncracked components (high-cycle fatigue)
- Tests at constant Δσ give an S–N curve (stress against cycles to failure, N_f, usually on log scales).
- Basquin's law: Δσ N_f^b = constant, with b typically about 0.07–0.13.
- Many steels show a fatigue (endurance) limit below which life appears indefinite; aluminium alloys generally do not, so a design life must be specified.
- A tensile mean stress shortens life. Goodman's rule: Δσ(σm) = Δσ(0) × (1 − σm/σts). Example: Δσ(0) = 300 MPa, σts = 600 MPa, σm = 200 MPa gives an allowable range of 200 MPa.
- Varying amplitudes: Miner's rule estimates failure when Σ N_i/N_fi = 1.
- Low-cycle fatigue (with plastic strain each cycle) follows the Coffin–Manson law: Δε_pl N_f^c = constant.

Cracked components
- In a structure that already contains a crack (e.g. a weld defect), life is the time to grow it to the critical size.
- Paris's law: da/dN = AΔK^m, with ΔK = YΔσ√(πa). For many metals m is about 2–4.
- Integrating from initial crack size a₀ to critical size a_c gives the life. For Y = 1 and m = 4: N = (1/a₀ − 1/a_c)/(AΔσ⁴π²).

Mechanisms
- Cracks usually start at the surface, at stress concentrations (holes, notches, scratches, inclusions), where cyclic slip produces persistent slip bands.
- They then grow perpendicular to the maximum principal stress, leaving beach marks visible to the eye and microscopic striations, one per cycle.
- Countermeasures: smooth surface finish, generous fillet radii, and compressive surface stresses (e.g. shot peening).

Weibull statistics for ceramics
Ceramics are brittle and contain flaws of random size, so their strength is scattered and depends on the volume stressed.
- Survival probability: P_s(V) = exp[−(V/V₀)(σ/σ₀)^m].
- m is the Weibull modulus. Larger m means less scatter. Typical ceramics have m of about 5–20; metals are far more consistent.
- At σ = σ₀ with V = V₀, P_s = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37.
- Size effect: for the same P_s, σ₂/σ₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(1/m). With m = 10, doubling the volume reduces the design stress by a factor of 2^(−0.1) ≈ 0.93, i.e. about 7%.
- Example: with m = 10, V = V₀ and σ = 0.9σ₀, P_s = exp(−0.9¹⁰) = exp(−0.349) ≈ 0.71, still a 29% chance of failure.
- Design for very low failure probabilities therefore needs stresses well below σ₀.

Exam tips: in Paris-law integrations, keep units consistent (ΔK in MPa√m, a in metres) and check that a_c is calculated from σmax and K_c, not from Δσ.

Friction and wear are surface properties: they depend on how two surfaces touch, not just on the bulk material.

Laws of friction
- The classic empirical laws: the friction force F is proportional to the normal load P, and independent of the apparent area of contact. The coefficient of friction is μ = F/P.
- Static friction (to start sliding) is usually somewhat higher than kinetic friction (to keep sliding).

Why the laws hold: real contact area
- All surfaces are rough on a microscopic scale. Two surfaces touch only at the tips of asperities, so the real area of contact A_r is a tiny fraction of the apparent area.
- The asperity tips deform plastically until they can carry the load: P ≈ A_r × H, where H is the hardness. So A_r ≈ P/H, proportional to load and independent of apparent area.
- Sliding requires shearing the junctions that form at these contacts (adhesion). If their shear strength is k, F ≈ kA_r, so μ ≈ k/H.
- With k ≈ σy/2 and H ≈ 3σy this gives μ of roughly 0.17. Measured values for clean dry metals are often larger because junctions grow under combined normal and shear load; this adhesion model is associated with Bowden and Tabor.
- Very clean metal surfaces in vacuum can cold-weld and seize.

Controlling friction
- Lubricants separate surfaces or provide a weak shear layer. In hydrodynamic lubrication a full fluid film supports the load; in boundary lubrication, molecular layers on the surfaces reduce adhesion. Both give much lower μ.
- Some solids have low friction because they shear easily: PTFE and graphite are classic examples.
- Where high friction is wanted (brakes, clutches, tyres), materials are chosen for a high and stable μ.

Wear
Wear is the loss of material from sliding surfaces.
- Adhesive wear: junctions form and shear inside the softer material, so fragments are torn off.
- Abrasive wear: hard particles or asperities plough or cut grooves in the softer surface.
- Archard's wear law: the volume worn per unit sliding distance is Q = KP/H, where K is a dimensionless wear coefficient. Material charts often use a related wear-rate constant instead (volume worn per unit sliding distance per unit load).
- So wear increases with load and sliding distance and decreases with hardness; hard surfaces (hardened steels, ceramics, hard coatings) resist wear.
- Surface treatments such as case hardening, nitriding and hard coatings improve wear resistance without changing the tough core.

Friction and wear in design
- Choose material pairs that do not adhere strongly (dissimilar materials, or a hard–soft pair as in plain bearings).
- Keep surfaces lubricated and clean, and keep abrasive particles out with seals and filters.

Exam tips: the key physical idea is that real contact area is set by load and hardness, not by apparent area; use it to explain both Amontons-type friction laws and Archard's wear law.

The last section of 1P2 brings environmental impact into materials choice. The 2025–26 syllabus lists environmental impact and life-cycle analysis as a lectured topic alongside selection.

Life-cycle thinking
A product's environmental burden comes from five phases:
- Material production: extracting and refining the material.
- Manufacture: shaping, joining and finishing.
- Transport: moving materials and products.
- Use: energy consumed during service (fuel, electricity).
- End of life: landfill, incineration, reuse or recycling, which may recover some of the embodied impact.

Measures used
- Embodied energy (MJ/kg): the energy to produce 1 kg of material from raw resources.
- Carbon footprint (kg CO₂ equivalent per kg).
- Other measures: water use, toxicity and resource depletion. Full life-cycle assessment (LCA) uses all of these; it is data-hungry, so designers often start with a simpler eco-audit based on energy and CO₂.

The eco-audit approach
1. Estimate the energy (or CO₂) for each life phase from a bill of materials, the manufacturing processes, transport distances and the use pattern.
2. Identify the dominant phase.
3. Target design changes at that phase, because effort spent on minor phases achieves little.

Which phase dominates?
- For products that consume energy in use over a long life (cars, aircraft, many appliances), the use phase usually dominates. Reducing mass, for example by substituting a lighter material, cuts use-phase energy, even if the lighter material has a higher embodied energy per kg.
- For products that use no energy in service (furniture, packaging, buildings' structural frames), the material production phase usually dominates, so choosing materials with low embodied energy, using less material and recycling matter most.

Trade-offs and examples
- Primary aluminium has several times the embodied energy per kg of steel, but it can save fuel in vehicles by reducing mass. Whether the switch pays off depends on how far the vehicle travels in its life.
- Recycled metals generally need much less energy than primary production, so recycled content and recyclability at end of life both matter.
- Composites such as CFRP save weight, but are harder to recycle.

Bringing it into selection
Environmental measures can be combined with the selection method in the next topic: replace cost per kg with embodied energy or CO₂ per kg in the objective function. For example, a light stiff beam that minimises embodied energy rather than mass maximises E^(1/2)/(H_m ρ), where H_m is the embodied energy per kg.

Exam tips: in an eco-audit question, set out a table of phases, estimate each one, and comment on the dominant phase; marks go for the reasoning and the design recommendation, not just the arithmetic.

notes.h: Material and process selection in design
notes.body:
Much of this material is delivered online in the 2025–26 syllabus, so work through the online units and examples paper carefully.

The selection method
1. Translation: state the function (e.g. a beam), the objective (e.g. minimise mass), the constraints (e.g. given stiffness and length) and the free variables (e.g. the cross-section size and the material).
2. Screening: eliminate materials that fail simple limits (temperature, corrosion, cost).
3. Ranking: use a material index derived from the objective.
4. Documentation: check the top candidates in more detail.

Deriving a material index
Light, stiff beam of square section b × b, length L, given stiffness S:
- S = C₁EI/L³ with I = b⁴/12 = A²/12.
- Mass m = ALρ. Eliminating the free variable A: m = (12S/C₁)^(1/2) L^(5/2) × ρ/E^(1/2).
- So minimise ρ/E^(1/2), i.e. maximise M = E^(1/2)/ρ.
Standard indices (maximise these):
- Light stiff tie: E/ρ. Light strong tie: σf/ρ.
- Light stiff beam: E^(1/2)/ρ. Light strong beam: σf^(2/3)/ρ.
- Light stiff panel (thickness free): E^(1/3)/ρ. Light strong panel: σf^(1/2)/ρ.
- To minimise cost, replace ρ by C_m ρ (cost per kg times density).

Using property charts
On log–log axes of E against ρ, a line of constant E/ρ has slope 1, constant E^(1/2)/ρ has slope 2 and constant E^(1/3)/ρ has slope 3. Slide the line towards the top left; materials above it are better.

Example
Steel (210 GPa, 7.8 Mg/m³), aluminium alloy (70 GPa, 2.7 Mg/m³), CFRP (taken as 100 GPa, 1.55 Mg/m³):
- E/ρ: 26.9, 25.9, 64.5. Steel and aluminium are about equal for ties.
- E^(1/2)/ρ: 1.86, 3.10, 6.45. For beams aluminium is clearly lighter than steel, and CFRP lighter still.

Shape and multiple constraints
- Shape factor for elastic bending φ = 12I/A², relative to a solid square (φ = 1). Tubes and I-sections have φ much greater than 1, and the index becomes (φE)^(1/2)/ρ.
- With two constraints (e.g. stiffness and strength), calculate the mass required to meet each; the larger one is the active constraint. With conflicting objectives (mass and cost), plot trade-off curves.

Manufacturing processes
- Families: shaping (casting, moulding, deformation such as forging and rolling, powder methods, composite forming, additive manufacturing), joining and surface treatment.
- Screen with process attribute charts: compatibility with the material, component mass, section thickness, tolerance and surface roughness, and economic batch size.

Cost of a batch-produced component
A simple model is C = mC_m/(1 − f) + C_t/n + Ċ_oh/ṅ: material (with scrap fraction f), tooling C_t spread over batch size n, and overhead rate (including capital) divided by production rate ṅ.
- Example: m = 0.5 kg, C_m = £4/kg, f = 0.1, C_t = £20,000, Ċ_oh = £60/h, ṅ = 30/h: C ≈ £24.22 each for n = 1000, but about £4.42 for n = 100,000.
- At small batches tooling dominates; at large batches material and overheads dominate, which explains why processes with expensive tooling (e.g. injection moulding, die casting) suit mass production.

Exam tips: always show the elimination of the free variable explicitly; the index is worth most of the marks, and a numerical ranking with a sentence of engineering judgement earns the rest.

questions.q: In a tensile test, the nominal stress is 400 MPa at a nominal strain of 0.20 (well beyond yield, before necking). Assuming constant volume, what is the true stress?
questions.why: σt = σn(1 + εn) = 400 × 1.2 = 480 MPa, because the area has shrunk to A₀/1.2. 333 MPa divides instead of multiplying; 400 MPa ignores the area change; 560 MPa has no basis.

questions.q: A Vickers hardness test on a metal gives H = 900 MPa. What is the best estimate of its yield strength?
questions.why: For metals H ≈ 3σy, so σy ≈ 900/3 = 300 MPa. 2700 MPa multiplies instead of dividing; 900 MPa ignores the constraint factor; 100 MPa uses a factor of 9.

questions.q: A metal specimen reaches a nominal stress of 400 MPa at a nominal strain of 0.20. Find the true stress and true strain, explaining any assumption, and explain why nominal stress falls after the tensile strength is reached even though the material is still work hardening.
markScheme: Assumes plastic flow at constant volume (AL = A₀L₀)
σt = σn(1 + εn) = 480 MPa
After the tensile strength, the area falls (necking) faster than the material hardens, so load and nominal stress fall
questions.modelAnswer: Plastic deformation conserves volume, so A = A₀L₀/L = A₀/(1 + εn). Hence σt = F/A = σn(1 + εn) = 400 × 1.2 = 480 MPa, and εt = ln(L/L₀) = ln 1.2 ≈ 0.18. The true stress keeps rising as the metal work hardens, but after the maximum load the reduction in cross-sectional area (localised necking) outweighs the rise in true stress, so the load, and with it the nominal stress F/A₀, falls.

questions.q: A steel bar (E = 210 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) is fixed between rigid walls with zero stress and then heated by 50 K. What is the stress in the bar?
questions.why: The bar wants to expand by αΔT = 6 × 10⁻⁴ but cannot, so σ = −EαΔT = −210 × 10⁹ × 6 × 10⁻⁴ = −126 MPa (compressive). It would be tensile on cooling; 12.6 MPa is a factor-of-ten slip; zero stress applies only if the bar is free.

questions.q: A material has E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.25. What is its shear modulus G?
questions.why: G = E/[2(1 + ν)] = 200/2.5 = 80 GPa. 100 GPa omits ν; 133 GPa is the bulk modulus E/[3(1 − 2ν)] = 200/1.5; 160 GPa uses E/(1 + ν).

questions.q: Equal-area bars of steel (E = 210 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) and aluminium alloy (E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) are joined rigidly at both ends with no initial stress and then heated by 100 K. Find the stress in each bar.
markScheme: Equilibrium: equal areas so stresses are equal and opposite (σ_s = −σ_a)
Compatibility: σ_s/E_s + α_sΔT = σ_a/E_a + α_aΔT
Solves σ = (α_a − α_s)ΔT/(1/E_s + 1/E_a)
σ ≈ 58 MPa
Steel in tension, aluminium in compression
questions.modelAnswer: With no external load and equal areas, the forces balance, so σ_s = −σ_a = σ. The bars stay the same length, so their total strains are equal: σ/E_s + α_sΔT = −σ/E_a + α_aΔT. Hence σ = (α_a − α_s)ΔT/(1/E_s + 1/E_a) = (11 × 10⁻⁶ × 100)/(4.76 × 10⁻¹² + 14.29 × 10⁻¹²) = 1.1 × 10⁻³/1.905 × 10⁻¹¹ ≈ 57.7 MPa. The aluminium wants to expand more, so it is held back (about 58 MPa compression) and the steel is stretched (about 58 MPa tension).

questions.q: How many atoms belong to one face-centred cubic unit cell?
questions.why: 8 corner atoms each shared by 8 cells give 1, and 6 face atoms each shared by 2 cells give 3: total 4. 2 is BCC; 14 counts the sites without sharing; 1 is simple cubic.

questions.q: Iron at room temperature is BCC with lattice parameter 0.2866 nm and atomic mass 55.85 g/mol. Its calculated density is closest to:
questions.why: ρ = 2 × 0.05585/(6.022 × 10²³ × (0.2866 × 10⁻⁹)³) ≈ 7.88 × 10³ kg/m³. 3.9 Mg/m³ uses 1 atom per cell; 15.8 Mg/m³ uses 4 (FCC counting); 2.7 Mg/m³ is aluminium.

questions.q: Copper is FCC with lattice parameter 0.3615 nm and atomic mass 63.55 g/mol. Calculate its density and its atomic radius.
markScheme: 4 atoms per FCC unit cell
ρ ≈ 8.94 × 10³ kg/m³
questions.modelAnswer: An FCC cell contains 4 atoms. Cell volume a³ = (3.615 × 10⁻¹⁰)³ ≈ 4.72 × 10⁻²⁹ m³. Mass of the atoms = 4 × 0.06355/6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 4.22 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. So ρ ≈ 4.22 × 10⁻²⁵/4.72 × 10⁻²⁹ ≈ 8.94 × 10³ kg/m³, close to the measured 8.96 Mg/m³. Atoms touch along a face diagonal, so 4r = √2 a and r = √2 × 0.3615/4 ≈ 0.128 nm.

questions.q: Glass fibres (E = 72 GPa) at volume fraction 0.5 in epoxy (E = 3 GPa) are loaded perpendicular to the fibres. The best simple estimate of the composite modulus is:
questions.why: Transverse loading puts both phases under the same stress, so 1/E = 0.5/72 + 0.5/3 = 0.1736 GPa⁻¹, giving E ≈ 5.8 GPa (the Reuss lower bound). 37.5 GPa is the equal-strain (longitudinal) bound; 14.7 GPa is the geometric mean √(72 × 3); 3.0 GPa ignores the fibres.

questions.q: An open-cell foam has relative density 0.2. According to the bending model, its Young's modulus as a fraction of the solid's is about:
questions.why: E/E_s ≈ (ρ/ρ_s)² = 0.2² = 0.04. A linear scaling (0.2) would apply if struts stretched rather than bent; 0.008 cubes the relative density; 0.45 is its square root.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of bonding, why the Young's modulus of a glassy polymer is much lower than that of a metal, and why it falls by orders of magnitude on heating through the glass transition temperature.
markScheme: E ≈ S/r₀: modulus set by bond stiffness
Metals: dense primary (metallic) bonds in all directions give E of order 100 GPa
Glassy polymer: covalent bonds along chains, but deformation is mostly taken by weak secondary (van der Waals/hydrogen) bonds between chains, giving a few GPa
Above Tg secondary bonds melt; chains can uncoil
Remaining stiffness from cross-links/entanglements is entropic, around 1–10 MPa for elastomers
questions.modelAnswer: Young's modulus reflects the stiffness of the bonds that are stretched: E ≈ S/r₀. In a metal every atom is held by strong metallic bonds in all directions, giving E of order 100 GPa. In a glassy polymer the chains have stiff covalent backbones, but they are tangled and randomly oriented, so most deformation stretches the weak secondary bonds between chains, which are much more compliant, giving E of a few GPa. At the glass transition the secondary bonds effectively melt and segments of chain can rotate freely. The only remaining resistance comes from entanglements or cross-links, and the stiffness is entropic (the chains resist being uncoiled), so the modulus drops by several orders of magnitude, to about 1–10 MPa in a cross-linked elastomer.

questions.q: Obstacles spaced 100 nm apart pin dislocations in a metal with G = 80 GPa and b = 0.25 nm. Using τ ≈ Gb/L and σy ≈ 3τy, the yield strength is about:
questions.why: τ = Gb/L = 80 × 10⁹ × 0.25 × 10⁻⁹/(100 × 10⁻⁹) = 200 MPa, and σy ≈ 3 × 200 = 600 MPa. 200 MPa is the shear stress τ without the Taylor factor of about 3; 67 MPa divides by 3; 6 GPa is a factor-of-ten slip.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT increase the yield strength of a metal?
options: Adding a fine dispersion of precipitates
questions.why: Annealing lets dislocations rearrange and annihilate (and grains recrystallise), removing work hardening and lowering yield strength. Smaller grains (Hall–Petch), cold work and fine precipitates all obstruct dislocations and raise strength.

questions.q: Explain why the measured yield strength of metals is far below their ideal strength, and describe two ways of strengthening an aluminium alloy, explaining the mechanism of each.
markScheme: Ideal strength from shearing whole planes is of order G/10
Real crystals yield by dislocation glide, breaking only one row of bonds at a time, at much lower stress
Strengthening means obstructing dislocations, τ ≈ Gb/L
Mechanism 1 described correctly (e.g. precipitation hardening by age hardening, with fine closely spaced particles)
Mechanism 2 described correctly (e.g. solid solution, work hardening or grain refinement)
questions.modelAnswer: Shearing a perfect crystal by sliding whole planes of atoms over each other requires breaking all the bonds across the plane at once, which needs a shear stress of order G/10. Real metals contain dislocations, which let slip proceed by breaking and remaking one row of bonds at a time, so plastic flow starts at stresses hundreds of times lower. Strength is raised by obstructing dislocations: if obstacles are spaced L apart, τ ≈ Gb/L. In aluminium alloys the main method is precipitation (age) hardening: the alloy is solution treated, quenched and then aged, so that fine, closely spaced precipitates form throughout the grains and pin dislocations. A second method is work hardening: cold rolling multiplies dislocations, which tangle and obstruct each other, raising strength at the cost of ductility. (Solid solution strengthening by dissolved magnesium, or grain refinement via Hall–Petch, would also earn credit.)

questions.q: A wide plate with a central crack (Y = 1) has K_c = 50 MPa√m and is loaded to 300 MPa. What is the critical crack half-length?
questions.why: a_c = (1/π)(K_c/σ)² = (1/π)(50/300)² = 0.0278/π ≈ 0.0088 m = 8.8 mm. 28 mm forgets to divide by π; 53 mm uses K_c/σ without squaring (0.167/π); 0.9 mm is a factor-of-ten slip.

questions.q: Which of these metals is most likely to show a ductile-to-brittle transition as the temperature falls?
questions.why: BCC metals such as ferritic steels show a marked drop in toughness at low temperature. Aluminium, copper and austenitic stainless steel are FCC and remain tough at low temperatures, which is why they are used for cryogenic equipment.

questions.q: A steel component with fracture toughness 50 MPa√m will contain cracks up to 2 mm long that cannot be detected (take K = σ√(πa) with a = 2 mm). (a) What is the maximum safe working stress against fast fracture? (b) The designer proposes a higher-strength steel with K_c = 25 MPa√m to save weight. Comment.
markScheme: σ_f = K_c/√(πa)
σ_f ≈ 630 MPa for K_c = 50 MPa√m
With K_c = 25 MPa√m, σ_f ≈ 315 MPa: halving K_c halves the fracture stress
Comments that higher yield strength is useless if fracture now governs; check both yield and fracture
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Fast fracture occurs when σ√(πa) = K_c, so σ_f = K_c/√(πa) = 50/√(π × 0.002) = 50/0.0793 ≈ 630 MPa. (In practice a safety factor would be applied.) (b) With K_c = 25 MPa√m the fracture stress halves to about 315 MPa. Although the new steel has a higher yield strength, the design would now be governed by fracture at a lower stress than before, so the weight saving may be illusory and the failure would be sudden and brittle. Both yield and fast fracture must be checked, and higher-strength alloys often have lower toughness.

questions.q: A ceramic has Weibull modulus 10. If the stressed volume is doubled, by roughly what factor must the design stress be reduced to keep the same survival probability?
questions.why: σ₂/σ₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(1/m) = (1/2)^(0.1) ≈ 0.93. 0.50 assumes stress scales inversely with volume; 0.97 uses 1/m = 0.05; 0.81 uses (1/2)^0.3.

questions.q: Using Goodman's rule, a steel with a fatigue range of 300 MPa at zero mean stress and σts = 600 MPa is used with a mean stress of 200 MPa. What is the allowable stress range?
questions.why: Δσ = 300 × (1 − 200/600) = 300 × 2/3 = 200 MPa. 300 MPa ignores the mean stress; 100 MPa subtracts the mean stress directly; 400 MPa adds the Goodman correction instead of subtracting it, 300 × (1 + 200/600).

questions.q: For a ceramic with Weibull modulus m = 10, tested on specimens of volume V₀ with σ₀ = 300 MPa: (a) find the survival probability of a specimen of volume V₀ at 270 MPa; (b) find the stress for which a component of volume 10V₀ has the same survival probability.
markScheme: P_s = exp[−(σ/σ₀)^m] for V = V₀
Same P_s requires (V/V₀)(σ/σ₀)^m constant, so σ₂ = σ₁(V₁/V₂)^(1/m)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For V = V₀, P_s = exp[−(σ/σ₀)^m] = exp[−(0.9)¹⁰] = exp(−0.349) ≈ 0.71, so about 29% of specimens fail. (b) The same survival probability requires (V/V₀)(σ/σ₀)^m to be unchanged, so 10 × σ₂^10 = 1 × 270^10, giving σ₂ = 270 × 10^(−1/10) = 270 × 0.794 ≈ 214 MPa. The larger component is more likely to contain a large flaw, so it must be designed to a lower stress.

questions.q: According to the adhesion model of friction, why is the friction force independent of the apparent area of contact?
options: Because the real contact area depends on the load and hardness, not on the apparent area
Because the surfaces are perfectly smooth
Because friction depends only on surface energy
Because the coefficient of friction is always 0.5
questions.why: Asperities deform plastically until A_r ≈ P/H, so the real contact area (and hence the friction force F ≈ kA_r) depends only on load and hardness. Real surfaces are rough, not smooth; surface energy alone does not explain the load dependence; μ varies widely between material pairs.

questions.q: By Archard's law, how does the wear volume change if the normal load doubles and the surface hardness is also doubled (all else equal)?
questions.why: Wear volume per unit sliding distance Q = KP/H. Doubling P and doubling H leaves P/H unchanged, so the wear volume is unchanged. Doubling only the load would double it; doubling only the hardness would halve it.

questions.q: Explain the physical basis of the laws of friction using the idea of real contact area, and use it to estimate a coefficient of friction for clean metal surfaces.
markScheme: Surfaces touch only at asperities; real area much smaller than apparent
Asperities yield: A_r ≈ P/H, proportional to load, independent of apparent area
Friction is the force to shear the junctions: F ≈ kA_r, so μ = k/H
With k ≈ σy/2 and H ≈ 3σy, μ ≈ 1/6 ≈ 0.17 (real values often higher due to junction growth)
questions.modelAnswer: Real surfaces are rough, so two surfaces in contact touch only at the tips of asperities. These deform plastically until their total area A_r can support the load: P ≈ HA_r, so A_r ≈ P/H, proportional to load and independent of the apparent area. Adhesive junctions form at these contacts, and sliding requires shearing them: F ≈ kA_r, where k is the shear strength of the junctions. Hence μ = F/P ≈ k/H. Taking k ≈ σy/2 and H ≈ 3σy gives μ ≈ 1/6 ≈ 0.17. Measured values for clean dry metals are often higher because junctions grow under the combined normal and tangential load.

questions.q: For a family car over its full life, which phase usually dominates energy consumption?
questions.why: Fuel burnt over the car's life usually far exceeds the energy embodied in its materials and manufacture. That is why lightweighting is a major strategy for vehicles. For products that use no energy in service, the material phase usually dominates instead; end of life can recover some energy through recycling.

questions.q: Which statement about replacing steel with aluminium in a vehicle body is most accurate?
options: It always reduces total life energy because aluminium is lighter
It always increases total life energy because aluminium has a higher embodied energy per kg
It can reduce total life energy if the fuel saved in use outweighs the extra embodied energy, which depends on lifetime distance
It has no effect because embodied energy is negligible
questions.why: Primary aluminium has several times the embodied energy per kg of steel, but the lighter body saves fuel throughout use. The net effect depends on the trade-off, and so on how far the vehicle travels; neither 'always' statement is correct, and embodied energy is not negligible.

questions.q: Describe the steps of an eco-audit for a product and explain how its result should guide design decisions, giving one example of a product dominated by the use phase and one dominated by the material phase.
markScheme: Lists life phases: material, manufacture, transport, use, end of life
Estimates energy/CO₂ for each phase from bill of materials, processes, transport and use pattern
Identifies the dominant phase and targets design changes there
Use-phase example (e.g. car, appliance) with strategy such as lightweighting or efficiency
Material-phase example (e.g. furniture, packaging) with strategy such as less material, low-embodied-energy or recycled materials
questions.modelAnswer: An eco-audit lists the product's life phases (material production, manufacture, transport, use and end of life) and estimates the energy or CO₂ for each, using a bill of materials with embodied energies, the manufacturing processes, transport distances and the energy used in service. The aim is to identify the dominant phase, because design changes there have the greatest effect. For a car the use phase (fuel) usually dominates, so reducing mass or improving efficiency matters most. For a product that uses no energy in service, such as a chair or packaging, material production usually dominates, so the designer should use less material, choose low-embodied-energy or recycled materials, and design for recycling.

questions.q: Which material index should be maximised to select a material for a light, stiff beam of square cross-section whose size is free?
questions.why: For a beam, stiffness ∝ EI ∝ EA², and eliminating A from m = ALρ gives m ∝ ρ/E^(1/2), so maximise E^(1/2)/ρ. E/ρ is for a tie; E^(1/3)/ρ for a panel of free thickness; σf/ρ for a strong tie.

questions.q: On a chart of log E against log ρ, a line of constant E^(1/2)/ρ has slope:
questions.why: E^(1/2)/ρ = M gives log E = 2 log ρ + 2 log M, a straight line of slope 2. Slope 1 is E/ρ and slope 3 is E^(1/3)/ρ.

questions.q: Derive the material index for a light, stiff tie of given length L that must carry a load F with an extension no greater than δ, and explain how the index is used with a property chart.
markScheme: Objective: m = ALρ; constraint: stiffness S = EA/L ≥ F/δ
Free variable A eliminated: A = SL/E
m = SL²(ρ/E), so maximise E/ρ
On log E vs log ρ chart, lines of constant E/ρ have slope 1
Move the line to the upper left; materials above it are the best candidates
questions.modelAnswer: The objective is to minimise the mass m = ALρ. The constraint is the stiffness: the extension δ = FL/(AE) must not exceed the limit, so S = EA/L ≥ F/δ. The free variable is the area A; eliminating it, A = SL/E, so m = SL²(ρ/E). S and L are fixed by the design, so the lightest tie maximises the index M = E/ρ. On a chart of log E against log ρ, lines of constant E/ρ are straight lines of slope 1. Sliding such a line towards the top left until only a few materials lie above it identifies the best candidates, which are then screened against other requirements such as cost and corrosion.

questions.q:
A wide steel plate contains a central through-crack and is subjected to a cyclic stress varying between 0 and 100 MPa. The steel has K_c = 50 MPa√m, and crack growth obeys da/dN = A(ΔK)⁴ with A = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ (ΔK in MPa√m, da/dN in m per cycle). Take K = σ√(πa), where a is the crack half-length.
(a) Find the critical crack half-length. [4]
(b) An initial crack of half-length 1 mm is present. Derive an expression for the number of cycles to failure and evaluate it. [8]
(c) Inspection can reliably detect cracks of half-length 5 mm. Recommend a maximum inspection interval, explaining your reasoning. [4]
(d) Describe how fatigue cracks typically start in an uncracked component and two ways of delaying initiation. [4]
markScheme: (a) Fast fracture uses σmax = 100 MPa: a_c = (1/π)(K_c/σmax)² ≈ 0.0796 m (79.6 mm)
(b) ΔK = Δσ√(πa) with Δσ = 100 MPa; da/dN = AΔσ⁴π²a²
(b) Separates variables and integrates: N = (1/(AΔσ⁴π²))(1/a₀ − 1/a_c)
(c) Growth from 5 mm to a_c: N ≈ (200 − 12.6)/9.87 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1.9 × 10⁴ cycles
(c) Interval must be well below this (e.g. half, about 9500 cycles) so a crack missed once is caught before failure
(d) Initiation at surface stress concentrations via persistent slip bands; remedies such as good surface finish, generous radii, shot peening (compressive surface stress)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Fast fracture occurs at the peak stress when σmax√(πa_c) = K_c, so a_c = (1/π)(K_c/σmax)² = (1/π)(50/100)² = 0.25/π ≈ 0.0796 m, i.e. about 80 mm.

(b) The stress range is Δσ = 100 MPa, so ΔK = Δσ√(πa) and da/dN = A(Δσ)⁴π²a². Separating variables: dN = da/(AΔσ⁴π²a²). Integrating from a₀ to a_c: N = (1/(AΔσ⁴π²)) ∫ from a₀ to a_c of a⁻² da = (1/(AΔσ⁴π²))(1/a₀ − 1/a_c). Here AΔσ⁴π² = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ × (100)⁴ × π² = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10⁸ × 9.870 ≈ 9.87 × 10⁻³ m⁻¹ per cycle. With a₀ = 0.001 m and a_c = 0.0796 m, 1/a₀ − 1/a_c = 1000 − 12.6 = 987.4 m⁻¹, so N ≈ 987.4/9.87 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵ cycles. Note that most of the life is spent while the crack is small: the 1/a_c term contributes little.

(c) A crack just too small to detect (5 mm) at one inspection must be found before it becomes critical. Its remaining life is N = (1/0.005 − 1/0.0796)/9.87 × 10⁻³ = (200 − 12.6)/9.87 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1.9 × 10⁴ cycles. The inspection interval must be less than this, with a margin for uncertainty in A, the load spectrum and detection reliability. A common approach is to inspect at no more than about half the remaining life, about 9500 cycles, so that a crack missed at one inspection still has a second chance of being found.

(d) In an uncracked component, cyclic plastic slip concentrates in persistent slip bands at the free surface, especially at stress concentrations such as holes, notches, scratches or inclusions; these form intrusions and extrusions that become microcracks, which then grow perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress. Initiation can be delayed by a smooth surface finish (polishing out scratches), generous fillet radii to reduce stress concentration, and introducing compressive residual surface stresses by shot peening or surface rolling.

questions.q:
A light, stiff cantilever beam of square cross-section (side b, free) and given length L must have a tip stiffness of at least S. Candidate materials are listed below; take the prices as given data for this question.
Steel: E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 Mg/m³, price £0.8/kg
Aluminium alloy: E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.7 Mg/m³, price £2.5/kg
CFRP: E = 100 GPa, ρ = 1.55 Mg/m³, price £40/kg
(a) Starting from S = C₁EI/L³ with I = b⁴/12, derive the material index to be maximised for minimum mass. [6]
(b) Calculate the mass of each design relative to steel. [5]
(c) Calculate the material cost of each design relative to steel, and derive the corresponding index. [5]
(d) Comment on the choice, including the effect of using a hollow tube rather than a solid section. [4]
markScheme: (a) m = ALρ with A = b²; I = A²/12 so S = C₁EA²/(12L³)
(a) Eliminates A: A = (12SL³/(C₁E))^(1/2); m = (12S/C₁)^(1/2) L^(5/2) ρ/E^(1/2); maximise E^(1/2)/ρ
(b) Relative to steel: Al ≈ 0.60, CFRP ≈ 0.29
(c) Cost ∝ C_m ρ/E^(1/2); index E^(1/2)/(C_m ρ)
(c) Relative cost: Al ≈ 1.9, CFRP ≈ 14
(d) Trade-off: CFRP lightest but most expensive, steel cheapest but heaviest, aluminium a compromise; choice depends on value of mass saving
(d) Hollow section increases shape factor φ = 12I/A² so index becomes (φE)^(1/2)/ρ; all materials benefit, limited by local buckling and manufacturability
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The objective is to minimise mass m = ALρ, where A = b². The constraint is the stiffness S = C₁EI/L³. For a square section I = b⁴/12 = A²/12, so S = C₁EA²/(12L³). The free variable is A: A = (12SL³/(C₁E))^(1/2). Substituting, m = (12SL³/(C₁E))^(1/2) × Lρ = (12S/C₁)^(1/2) L^(5/2) × ρ/E^(1/2). S, L and C₁ are fixed by the design, so the mass is minimised by minimising ρ/E^(1/2), i.e. maximising M₁ = E^(1/2)/ρ.

(b) Mass ∝ ρ/E^(1/2) (E in GPa, ρ in Mg/m³): steel 7.8/√210 = 7.8/14.49 ≈ 0.538; aluminium 2.7/√70 = 2.7/8.37 ≈ 0.323; CFRP 1.55/√100 = 0.155. Relative to steel: aluminium ≈ 0.60, CFRP ≈ 0.29. The aluminium beam is 40% lighter and the CFRP beam about 70% lighter than steel.

(c) Material cost = m × C_m ∝ C_mρ/E^(1/2), so the index for minimum cost is M₂ = E^(1/2)/(C_mρ). Values of C_mρ/E^(1/2): steel 0.8 × 0.538 ≈ 0.431; aluminium 2.5 × 0.323 ≈ 0.807; CFRP 40 × 0.155 = 6.2. Relative to steel: aluminium ≈ 1.9, CFRP ≈ 14.

(d) There is a trade-off: steel is cheapest but heaviest, CFRP lightest but by far the most expensive, and aluminium is intermediate on both. The right choice depends on how much a unit of mass saved is worth: in aerospace or racing applications the CFRP mass saving may justify its cost; for a building or general machinery steel is likely to win; aluminium suits transport applications where mass matters moderately. Using a hollow tube instead of a solid square raises the shape factor φ = 12I/A² well above 1, so the same stiffness needs less material and the index becomes (φE)^(1/2)/ρ. All three materials benefit, but the achievable φ is limited by local buckling of thin walls and by what can be manufactured, which differs between metals and composites. Other factors such as joining, corrosion, damage tolerance and environmental impact would also be considered before a final choice.
